🎯 Serving Architecture: First Token vs Output Throughput (One Request)
Pilot one-request runs (c=1, 21 Sep archive), one point per layout: mean first token (s) against output tok/s, at 128K or 1M (chips). Single-node layouts ran on one node, two-node layouts on the native fabric. Click a point to open its run.
Executive TakeawayTP4/PP4 has both the lowest first token (1.71 s at 128K, 28.57 s at 1M) and the highest output rate (30.99 tok/s at 128K, 1.11 tok/s at 1M), so at one request it beats every other layout on both axes. There is no trade-off curve here, only one point that dominates. It uses 16 GPUs; TP4/PP1 uses 4.
Read With CareAt one request the two axes move together: tok/s is the output tokens over the request's own time, most of which is the first token. At 128K the single-node runs generated 128 output tokens per request and the two-node runs 64, so their tok/s are not like-for-like; at 1M all six generated 32.
⏱️ First-Token Wall-Time Budget by Layout (§4.17 Architecture Spectrum)
Share of the mean first-token time (one request, pilot) spent in prefill collectives, pipeline waits, prefill kernels and outside the engine, per layout at 8K, 128K and 1M. † and lighter bars: modelled split (the measured per-call collective time × calls per chunk), as the time-budget table marks every 1M row and TP8/PP1 8K; the other splits are measured from per-rank captures.
FIRST TOKEN · 1M MODELLED
Regime ShiftFirst token only: at 8K, collectives take 54 % of TP4/PP1's first token (0.1197 of 0.2222 s, measured). At 1M, prefill kernels take 83 % of it (77.17 of 93.25 s), a split the time-budget table marks modelled.
Decode Is DifferentAn 8K decode token has its own budget: 23 % AllReduce on TP4/PP1 (24 % with all collectives). Cross-node TP16/PP1 spends 75 % of its 128K first token in collectives (measured) and 44 % at 1M (modelled), where kernels take 54 %.

🧱 Campaign Scope / Gaps
Known before metrics are loaded.
Application E2E: GCP_NATIVE + configured-100G + configured-20G measured (119 completed runs). All native topology, long-context, scheduler/KV, compute, NCCL, telemetry and profiler evidence surfaced when present.
Hardware Microbench: Native + 100G + 50G + 20G + 10G measured via iperf/NCCL.
Not established / Unresolved: Application E2E at 50G/10G, local physical 2×10GbE equivalence, two-node decode profiles (single-node graphs-on decode profiles exist; multi-node decode points were captured but their per-worker exports failed: usable 2/8, 2/16, 0/16, 0/9), two-node serving under load in the pilot (it ran all 36 two-node runs one request at a time; stage 2 ran the four layouts at 8K c8, 128K c2–c8 and 1M c2/c4 in another session: Scale-Out [5.2]), and minimum production bandwidth threshold.

📡 Prefill Communication Share by Prompt Length — The Number Behind "Comm Isn't the HW Bottleneck" (§4.4)
An 8K prefill chunk executes 55 AllReduces of 8,192 × 2,304 × 2 B = 37.7 MB. nccl-tests (TP4 native): 19.0 µs @ 16 KiB, 17.4 GB/s algbw @ 256 MiB → α-β time ≈ 2.19 ms. In eager prefill capture (tp4_prefill), 880 prefill-chunk calls = 2.18 ms/call (α-β estimate within 1%). Chunk compute scales quadratically with prefix; AllReduce communication cost does not.
EMPIRICAL FABRIC SHARE
Prompt Length8K ChunksAllReduce Time per RankTTFT (Serving TP4)Comm ShareEmpirical Mechanism & Hardware Architectural Impact
8K1≈ 0.12 s0.222 s54 %Intra-node PCIe ring bus bandwidth (26 GB/s, no NVLink) makes AllReduce 54% of 8K TTFT. Faster fabric helps here.
128K161.92 s measured (nsys: 2.06s incl 7 decode steps)4.53 s≈ 42 %TP8 takes 2.56s AllReduce (51–55% share) in 4.66s capture: per GPU, non-collective kernel time fell only 23% (2.415 → 1.851 s; MoE flat at 0.640 → 0.646 s) while collectives grew 24% (2.059 → 2.561 s), so per-GPU kernel time barely moves (4.47 → 4.41 s) while the first token is 0.28 s slower on 8 GPUs (4.53 s → 4.81 s); the slowdown lies outside the per-GPU kernel sums.
512K64≈ 7.7 s (extrapolated @ 0.12s/chunk)31.9 s≈ 24 %Attention compute scales quadratically with position over prefix; collective communication share drops to 24%.
1M122≈ 14.6 s (extrapolated)93.3 s≈ 16 %Chunk compute completely dominates first token (83% kernels); communication is definitively not the hardware bottleneck.
Hardware Bottleneck Quantification: On this PCIe host (26 GB/s ring busbw, no NVLink), intra-node TP prefill spends 16–57% of first token in AllReduce depending on prompt length, while cross-node TP16 spends 77.6% of its kernel time in collectives (12 usable ranks; 75% of its 128K first token). For PP boundaries, SendRecv waits consume 8–22% of kernel time at 128K and about 26% on stage 0 at 512K (§4.7). These three numbers answer where faster fabric helps: TP within a node for short prompts, yes; PP across nodes, no.

🚫 What Not To Do
Promote as measured lessons only when performance characterization evidence supports them
Do not choose topology from peak tokens/sec alone.
Do not call admission success production capacity.
Do not assume “fits in VRAM” means usable latency.
Do not assume prefill and decode prefer the same topology.
Do not extrapolate 128K behavior linearly to 1M.
Do not extrapolate beyond the measured Native / configured-100G / configured-20G points; do not infer 50G/10G application behavior or local 2×10GbE equivalence without runs.
Do not infer NCCL/PP causality from E2E latency alone.
Do not compare unmatched workload conditions.
Do not use profiler-instrumented latency as normal benchmark latency.
Do not treat CUTLASS reference as model-kernel efficiency.
Do not tune scheduler knobs blindly if another subsystem dominates.
Do not render missing / unresolved evidence as zero.

1. Fabric Exposure

Topology Dependent

The same measured fabric constraint produces radically different user-visible TTFT damage depending on topology.

Key Measured Finding 1M · configured-20G vs GCP_NATIVE

Why It Matters
Fabric capability alone does not determine serving impact. The scale-out topology determines how much transport degradation is exposed to application TTFT. Network sizing must be driven by measured application exposure, not raw NIC/iperf bandwidth alone.
Confidence Semantics
Evidence Metric: HIGH
Causal Mechanism: MEDIUM-HIGH
Direct empirical measurement under GCP Native (~173.58 Gb/s), Capped 100G (56.84 Gb/s), and Capped 20G (16.48 Gb/s) across 4 distributed topologies.

Secondary Evidence
Key Architectural Takeaways
  • Fabric sensitivity varies dramatically by topology: scale-out design cannot be treated as a single uniform class.
  • TP16/PP1 is severely exposed to transport degradation because AllReduce collectives are serialized over the cross-node fabric on every layer (+188.69s tax @ 1M).
  • TP4/PP4 is far less sensitive in the same 1M cap condition (+3.91% TTFT) because cross-node boundaries use point-to-point Send/Recv pipelining.
  • Small negative TP8/PP2 deltas (-0.10% @ 1M) are signed observations; do not call them noise without replicate variance.
⚡ Architectural Decision Changed
Choose and size scale-out topology from measured application exposure to transport degradation, not NIC/iperf capability alone.
Boundary: No 8K application cap sweep; no 50G/10G application claim; configured network label != measured achieved bandwidth; no universal topology winner.

📊 Multi-Node Concurrency Scaling: c=1 vs c=2 vs c=4 (First Token ÷ Own Prefill Time)
Mean first token ÷ the same run's mean engine prefill time, so each bar is read against its own session. Dashed line: (N+1)/2, the value when N prompts sent together are prefilled one at a time. c=1: the pilot's one-request runs (21 Sep archive). c=2 / c=4: stage 2 (stage2/03_multi_node_load, 6 Oct), which ran a different MoE backend (FlashInfer CUTLASS, autotune off) and a different vLLM build, on other GPUs of the same type. Seconds in the tooltips.
Context:
ObservationAt 1M each run is one wave (2 or 4 prompts), and all four layouts sit on the serial law: 1.50–1.52× their own prefill time at c=2 and 2.45–2.48× at c=4 (c=1, pilot: 1.02–1.05×). TP4/PP4 behaves like TP16/PP1. At 128K the c=2 / c=4 runs are closed loops over 5 waves, so the law is only a guide there: 1.46–1.47× at c=2, 1.71–2.28× at c=4.
Key FindingPipeline stages do not admit two long prefills at once: the two-node layouts take long prompts one at a time, as one node does, and no layout absorbs a prefill burst. Long-prompt concurrency has to come from replicas; a chunk cap (--long-prefill-token-threshold), which would let two reads share a step, is untested.
📈 Concurrency Scaling: c=1 vs c=2 vs c=4 (Token Throughput & TPOT)
Output tok/s (bars) and mean TPOT (lines, ms). c=1: the pilot's one-request run (21 Sep archive). c=2 / c=4: stage 2 (stage2/03_multi_node_load, 6 Oct), which ran a different MoE backend (FlashInfer CUTLASS, autotune off) and a different vLLM build, on other GPUs of the same type, so the step from c=1 to c=2 mixes the session into the effect.
c=1 PILOT · c=2/4 STAGE 2
ObservationAt 128K, TP4/PP4 serves 30.99 tok/s at c=1 and 32.67 / 36.88 tok/s at c=2 / c=4, while its mean TPOT rises to 21.40 / 46.28 ms (median ITL 10.02 / 13.07 ms). TP16/PP1 serves 8.69 / 9.40 / 9.71 tok/s. At 1M, output does not grow with concurrency on any layout (TP4/PP4 1.11 → 1.11 → 1.13 tok/s): the long prompts are prefilled one at a time.
Sessionc=1 and c=2 / c=4 come from different sessions. TP8/PP2's 1M output falls from 0.76 to 0.69 tok/s because its stage-2 engine prefill is slower, 46.4–46.8 s against 40.1 s in the pilot (inferred); the other layouts do not move. Compare layouts within one column.

⚡ PP2 15/12 Layer Split (Stage 2 A/B: Decode −0.2% to −1.2%; First Token +3.1% to −5.6%)
Asymmetric pipeline stage layer partitioning (15 layers on Stage 0 vs. 12 layers on Stage 1), set as VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=15,12 in node 0's recorded environment; no log shows the stage layer ranges, and the changed first tokens suggest it applied (inferred). PCI Bus & Socket Mapping (from node inventory): GPUs 0–3 sit on Socket 0 (PCI buses 05/06/0A/0B); GPUs 4–7 sit on Socket 1 (PCI buses 84/85/89/8A). 🔬 Repeatability Noise Floor (§4.11): Eight pairs of identical configurations across the campaign establish the empirical dashboard noise floor: TTFT agrees within 0.03–0.5% at c1 and within 1.9–4.98% under load (8K c8, 128K c4); TPOT agrees within 0.02–3.08%. Deltas of ±0.10% (e.g. TP8/PP2 at 1M: −0.10%, or TP4/PP2 at 1M under 100G: +0.13%) are within pure replicate noise; +1.14% (TP4/PP2 at 20G, 1M) is at the statistical boundary; +3.91% (TP4/PP4 at 20G, 1M) and +14.67% (TP4/PP4 at 20G, 128K) are empirically verified network slowdowns.

(2) Power reveals true work: TP16 at 80.6% "utilization" draws 225 W (busy spinning on AllReduce sync) while TP4/PP4 at 62.8% draws 310 W (real compute). (3) In every PP layout, Node 1 draws 17–21% more power than Node 0 at 1M (414 vs 343 W, 337 vs 282 W, 289 vs 247 W) because later stages hold more full-attention layers (§4.7).
⚖️ Pipeline-Stage Imbalance (16-Rank Exports) — Real, Measurable, and Structural (§4.7)
Profiles from profiles_multi_node_native/tp4_pp4_dist/long_prefill_512k (16 usable ranks, grouped by AllReduce counts 1,143 / 1,067 / 1,067 / 915 = stages 0–3; 27 layers split 7/7/7/6). Corrected in v1.1.
STRUCTURAL IDLE
Stage (Node / GPUs)Flash-Attention TimeSendRecv Waiting TimeShare of 10.5s Run Spent WaitingStructural Layer Breakdown
Stage 0 (Node 0, GPUs 0–3)2.37 s (1 full-attn layer: #3)2.75–2.77 s26 %7 layers (0–6). Holds only ONE full-attention layer (#3). Half the attention compute of other stages!
Stage 1 (Node 0, GPUs 4–7)4.71 s (layers #7, #11)0.40–0.44 s4 %7 layers (7–13). Holds TWO full-attention layers (#7, #11). Balanced compute.
Stage 2 (Node 1, GPUs 8–11)4.71 s (layers #15, #19)0.50–0.53 s5 %7 layers (14–20). Holds TWO full-attention layers (#15, #19). Balanced compute.
Stage 3 (Node 1, GPUs 12–15)4.71 s (#23, #26) + lm_head1.10–1.13 s11 %6 layers (21–26). Holds TWO full-attention layers (#23, #26) plus lm_head. Waits 11% on upstream.
v1.1 Correction & Cost Model: Equal layer counts ≠ equal work when attention cost scales with context! The 7 full-attention layers sit at #3, #7, #11, #15, #19, #23, #26. A two-parameter cost model (0.61s/layer + 2.36s/full-attn layer at 512K) reproduces measured busy time of every stage within 5% (model: 6.6 / 9.0 / 9.0 / 8.4s vs measured 6.3 / 9.1 / 8.9 / 8.5s). Because full-attention layers sit every 4th layer, any contiguous partition of ≥ 8 layers picks up two attention layers; stage 0 cannot absorb an 8th layer without picking up layer #7. Scoring all 2,600 contiguous splits of 27 layers into 4 with this cost model predicts that none beats 7/7/7/6 (partition 8,7,6,6 is predicted to make stage 0 heaviest and raise TTFT by +7%). The 26% stage-0 idle is structural for PP4 and must be priced, not tuned. Where the model predicts a gain: In PP2, partition 15,12 (vs default 14,13) is predicted to cut stage-0 idle 10% → 3% and shorten 512K TTFT by 3.5% on TP4/PP2 (cost-model prediction, not a pilot measurement; stage 2 measured −1.9% on TP4/PP2 and −4.3% on TP8/PP2 at 512K in another session: Scale-Out [5.3]).
Independent Confirmation (PP2 Check — §6.2): The two PP2 128K captures independently confirm the 3:4 attention split predicted by the layer map: Stage 0 / Stage 1 flash attention time ratio is 0.77 on TP4/PP2 (8 usable ranks) and 0.77 on TP8/PP2 (15 usable ranks), closely corroborating (within 3% of 0.75) the 0.75 ratio expected from the 3 vs 4 full-attention layer distribution (of 7 total layers: #3, #7, #11 vs #15, #19, #23, #26).

Hardware Architecture Takeaway: Intra-node numbers confirm the server is PCIe-class (52 GB/s per GPU pair, 26 GB/s ring busbw; NVLink systems provide 10–20× higher bandwidth). Cross-node TP16 decode is governed purely by network latency α (~208–290 µs per collective across VPC), while prefill is bandwidth-bound β (3.5× lower bandwidth under 20G cap directly inflates 128K TTFT from 6.42s to 31.05s (+383.7%)).

Critical Architectural Discovery: Peak KV cache usage increases modestly from ~12.2% to ~15.5%, remaining far below memory exhaustion, and Preemptions remain 0 across all loads. (Note: On TP8 c4, first tokens arrived at 75.0s, 148.3s, 294.7s, 221.6s in request order; the four requests left the client 0 / 20 / 40 / 59 ms apart, so the order in which the engine received them is not recorded, and these times do not show out-of-order scheduling.) The latency degradation is overwhelmingly prefill-compute and scheduling-queue bound: simultaneous requests get first token sequentially one full prefill apart (at 1M c4: 93.5s, 185.4s, 277.3s, 368.9s; at 512K c4: 32.0s, 63.9s, 95.6s, 127.2s) as vLLM serializes long prefills (peak_running = 2, peak_waiting = 3). Derived queue-accounting indicates that added queue residence accounts for ~96.4% (c1→c2) and ~97.5% (c1→c4) of added TTFT on TP4, and ~95.7% (c1→c2) and ~97.2% (c1→c4) on TP8. Production admission limits depend on explicit application SLOs; c=1 is the cleanest measured single-node operating point.

Exact miss counts: 128K: 7 of 7 repeats hit (87.33%); 512K: 2 of 3 repeats hit (49.98% — the missed request had 524,545 tokens against 524,544; cause not confirmed); 1M: 2 of 3 repeats hit (49.97% — the missed request had the same 1M tokens; cause not recorded). Prefix caching provides substantial latency reduction for workloads with repeated-prefix reuse; production value depends on hit rate and cache residency.

Four Critical Readings: (1) Single requests never queue; time outside the engine core is 1–11% of their first token, up to 11.35% on TP4/PP4 at 128K (14 ms at 8K, growing with prompt length due to tokenization/transfer). (2) First token is collective-bound on TP4 at 8K (54%) and on TP16 (75% at 128K, against 42.3% on TP4 at 128K), and kernel-bound for long prompts on TP4/PP1 (74–83% at 512K–1M; 44.4–78.1% on the other layouts). (3) Under load, wall time is scheduler-dominated: queueing is 50% of first token at 128K c4 and 58% at 1M c4; waiting behind other requests' prefills is 86–96% of decode time at long contexts. (4) 1M decode on TP4: 59% memory floor at the 1.60 TB/s bus ceiling (weights + KV; the KV alone 49%), 46% on TP8, 26% on TP16 (the table above and view 2 price memory at BabelStream's 1.72 TB/s: 54 / 43 / 25%); PP2 pays 5–6% of the first token in pipeline waits at the stage boundary vs 12–13% for PP4 (a decode token's hops at 1M: 2.6–3.5%); TP16 cross-node collective is ~208 µs/call.

🔍 FP8 KV-Cache on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120): Server Did Not Start, Cause Not Logged
Unconfirmed explanation for the V8 `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` startup failure on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120). FP8 was attempted three times (two pilot cases, one stage-2 rerun); server exited rc=1 after 132, 134 and 184 s; no log. The stage-2 rerun (stage2/01_fp8_kv_rerun, 6 Oct) added use_prefill_query_quantization: true.
HYPOTHESIS · NOT RUN

Hypothesis from engine source (not from this run's log): In vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py, vLLM strictly validates backend_supports_prefill_query_quantization():

if not current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100):
    return False # Strictly requires GB200/B200 SM100 Architecture

1. Hardware Generation: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition is SM120 (capability 12.0). Because is_device_capability_family(100) strictly returns False, vLLM rejects prefill query quantization.
2. MLA Head Dimensions: Kimi-Linear-48B uses Multi-Head Latent Attention with head dimensions (128, 64, 128) in the archive's model config (qk_nope 128, qk_rope 64, v 128; q/k head 192): the set this card lists as FlashInfer-supported, so head dimensions do not explain the failure. The card's other backend claims (TRT-LLM Ragged without SM120 binaries; FlashAttention-4 BF16/FP16 only) belong to the unconfirmed explanation and were not checked.
3. Status: not confirmed. Whether FP8 KV-Cache for Kimi-Linear-48B needs SM100 hardware is not shown: point 1 limits one optimisation (prefill-query quantization), and no failing run's own error line is on file. The stage-2 rerun with that quantization switched on also exited rc=1 (184 s), which fits the explanation but does not test it. Until the server log is read, the V8 failure stays NOT_RUN (rc=1) with its cause unlogged.

⚡ Chunk-Size / Prompt Budget Finding (8K at c4)
The 8K first token doubles at c4 (0.21s → 0.42s own prefill) while queue is only 27 ms. Because prompt length (8,192) equals max_num_batched_tokens, a single active decode token forces the prompt into a 2nd chunk that waits behind the next prompt's first chunk. Stage 1 tested a budget of 8,448 (5 Oct, stage1/01_chunk_budget_ab; another session than the pilot, so it is compared only with its own 8,192 control, the same prompts in the same order): 11 of the 22 comparable c4 requests reach the first token one chunk step (~0.2 s) earlier, 3 one step later and 8 at the same time. Over those 22 requests the c4 mean falls 13.1% (601.0 → 522.3 ms; the control's two 4.6 s first-wave requests are left out), and the c32 mean 6.2% (1,618.1 → 1,517.6 ms, all 128 requests). The predicted ~211 ms is one chunk step, not the mean saving.
🧠 MoE Decode Batching & Expert Expansion Finding
Under load, MoE decode step expands from 4.5 ms (c1, 8 active experts) to 15.8 ms (c32, ~163 of 256 experts expected under uniform routing) and 22.9 ms at full load (~222 experts). Routed weights read at memory speed grow from 0.9 ms to 10.5 and 14.9 ms, while kernels above the floor stay at 2.5–4.7 ms. By c16, decode is memory-bound on weights rather than KV, explaining why throughput scales sub-linearly with concurrency.
🛑 Decode Stalls Behind Other Requests' Prefill Chunks — How Much of Per-Token Wait is Interference (§4.5)
Campaign Scope: Single-node local execution (TP4/PP1 & TP8/PP1). In the pilot, distributed layouts (TP4/PP2, TP8/PP2, TP4/PP4, TP16/PP1) were run at c=1 only. Stage 2 ran them under load (8K c8, 128K c2/c4/c8, 1M c2/c4; stage2/03_multi_node_load, 6 Oct) with FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE with autotune off (pilot: Triton) and a different vLLM build, on other GPUs of the same type: see Scale-Out.
Per-token inter-token latencies (itls list in benchmark JSONs; first entry skipped). A "stall" is an ITL > 100 ms. Co-scheduled prefills freeze ongoing decodes for about one chunk at 8K (stall median 207.8 ms vs a 222.2 ms chunk); at 1M a stall is about half a chunk (inferred).

Architectural Takeaway: Quantifies the prefill/decode disaggregation case without new experiments: at 8K load, decode SLO is dictated by prefill chunk interference, not batch compute. Explains the chunk size trade-off: 16K chunks at 128K c4 gave lower mean TPOT than 4K chunks (105 vs 141 ms; stalls 649 → 132). Against the 8K default (119.3 ms), stalls fall 304 → 132 while each one doubles (276 → 538 ms). Remedies: decode-priority scheduling, separate P/D pools, or admission control gated by "prefill chunks in flight".

⚠️ Client-Side Concurrency Cap Caveat (§4.13): tp4_openloop_8192 ran with --max-concurrency 64, and tp4_openloop_131072 with --max-concurrency 32. Achieved request rate saturates at 3.30–3.42 req/s (8K) and 0.183–0.185 req/s (128K) from 0.90× onward while offered rate climbs to 5.29 / 0.285 req/s. At 8K the excess requests queue in the benchmark client, invisible to server-side TTFT; at 128K each rate sent 24 prompts under the cap of 32, so the cap cannot bind and the queue is server-side (4.7 s at 0.90×, 15.7–16.1 s at 1.00–1.25×). Consequently, the 8K server queue_mean stays ≤ 0.254 s, 8K TTFT shows non-monotonicity above the knee (979 → 784 → 826 ms), and the real unconstrained cliff is steeper than shown. (The knee location at 0.90× / 0.75× remains empirically sound as it occurs below the client cap).

📍 Capacity Knee / Admission Decision
Candidate Knee location (Heuristic: slope inflection of TPOT / queue degradation)8K: ~0.90x offered load (~3.811 RPS offered, ~3.302 req/s achieved; queue 0.182s, TPOT 60.86ms) · 128K: ~0.75x offered load (~0.171 RPS; queue 1.94s, TPOT 50.57ms)
Leading Measured Operating Point (SLO Objective Dependent)8K: c≤8 closed-loop (TPOT 10.82ms mean / 13.28ms p95, queue 0.19s) · 128K: ≤0.50x offered load for p95 TPOT ≤ 100ms (~0.114 RPS, TTFT 7.51s, queue 2.52s, p95 TPOT 95.5ms; at 0.75x p95 TPOT is 145.3ms) · 1M: c=1 cleanest measured point (TTFT 74.69s TP8 / 93.25s TP4, context baselines; queue ~0.00s)
What breaks firstQueue wait time and TPOT degrade simultaneously before memory exhaustion: at 1M c2 queue reaches 35.3s (TP8) / 44.3s (TP4) and TPOT increases to 177.2ms / 182.0ms while KV (15.3–15.5%) and preemptions (0) remain stable
DecisionWorkload-scoped candidate admission limits: for 1M interactive/SLO workloads, admit at c=1 (cleanest measured single-node point); for 8K interactive decode, evaluate c≤8 to keep TPOT ~10.8ms depending on target SLO; for 128K open-loop, evaluate throttling admission beyond 0.50× (~0.114 RPS) to hold p95 TPOT ≤ 100 ms (145.3 ms at the 0.75× candidate knee), well before the 1.00× queuing cliff.
Confidence—
Evidenceclosed-loop + open-loop + Prometheus

First token: compute, collectives, pipeline waits, queueing and overhead, by layout, prompt and load
Engine histograms (queue, prefill) + the client's mean first token per run, six layouts; prefill split from the captures, or from the per-call collective time where marked †; one request unless a load is shown. Thin segments (†) are the modelled part of the split; full-height segments are measured, or differences of measured times.
queue: waiting for admissionpipeline waits (SendRecv)prefill collectives (AllReduce)prefill kernels: attention, GEMM, MoEsteps shared with other requests (their decode, their chunks)outside the engine: tokenise · transfer · API server · schedule · sample
full height: measured, or a difference of measured timesthin, †: the modelled part of the split (hover for how)
† modelled split: the measured per-call AllReduce time (one-node 128K Nsight captures: 2.18 ms TP4, 2.71 ms TP8; TP16's usable 512K rank: 4.47 ms) × the calls per chunk; PP2 waits from the stage cost model plus the pipeline fill; TP4/PP4 · 1M from its 512K capture's shares. Full-height prefill segments: the captures' collective and SendRecv shares, and kernels = the engine's prefill − those.
Overhead outside the engine grows with the prompt: 14 ms at 8K, 0.19 s at 128K, 1.4 s at 1M (tokenise + transfer); so does the kernel share, because attention grows with position.
Under load the request's own prefill stretches (+0.35 s at 8K full load, +0.52 s at 128K c4): its steps are shared with others' decode and chunks (view 3). Queue = arrival → first scheduled step.

E2E · WHERE A DECODE TOKEN'S TIME GOES
Decode token: collectives, memory-speed floor, kernels above it, pipeline hops, waiting behind prefills
The client's mean inter-token time per run, six layouts; split: the graphs-on torch budget at 8K + KV bytes at memory speed; loaded rows: own step = median normal token, the rest waits. Thin segments (†) are the modelled part of the split; full-height segments are measured, or differences of measured times.
collectives (AllReduce)pipeline hops (PP)memory-speed floor: weights + KV bytes ÷ 1.72 TB/skernels above the floor (compute, launch, small-batch tails)waiting behind other requests' prefill chunks
full height: measured, or a difference of measured timesthin, †: the modelled part of the split (hover for how)
† modelled: the memory-speed floor (weights + KV bytes at 1.72 TB/s; the KV alone 8.1 GB per token at 1M = 4.7 ms at 1.72 TB/s) and the kernels above it (the token's remainder) on every row; beyond 8K the collectives too (the 8K torch value carried over); PP rows take these from the same-width one-node row. Measured growth 8K → 1M: 5.8 ms (TP4), 5.8 (TP8); TP16, which has no 8K run: 5.1 ms from 128K to 1M.
The latent is replicated on every rank, so the long-context read costs the same at any width: at 1M the token is memory-bound on its cache; only fewer bytes (FP8 KV) help.
TP16 collective = remainder after kernels and floor: 208 µs per call at 128K, 512K and 1M alike (nccl-tests' 16 KiB point: 290 µs; a decode call is 4.6 KB). Loaded rows: view 4.

cN = closed loop, N in flight · open loop x× = arrivals at x × a reference rate (8K 4.23, 128K 0.228 req/s; served traffic tops out near 0.8×) · c1 = anchor. Thin segments (†) are the modelled part of the split; full-height segments are measured, or differences of measured times.
queue: waiting for admissionprefill collectives (AllReduce)prefill kernels: attention, GEMM, MoEsteps shared with other requests (their decode, their chunks)outside the engine: tokenise · transfer · API server · schedule · sample

† TP8's collectives, and TP4's at 512K–1M, from the measured per-call time × the calls per chunk (as in view 1). The engine's split is the single request's: a chunk does the same work under load, it only shares its step.
Queue (arrival → first scheduled step): 84% of the first token at 128K c16 (31 of 37 s), 58% at 1M c4: prefills are serialised, the backlog sets the wait. Outside the engine: 15 → 232 ms (8K).
Closed loop sends its first N requests together, a burst that never recurs: at 8K c32 the first 32 average 3.7 s, the 96 after them 0.94 s (128K c8: 20.3 vs 8.8 s); bars are run means.

⚡ Finding 1: 8K First Token Doubles at c4 Due to Chunk Boundary
Own prefill surges 0.21s → 0.42s (2.0×) at c4 while queue is only 27 ms: the 8,192-token prompt exactly matches max_num_batched_tokens. When even one decode token shares the forward step, the prompt is forced into a second chunk whose tail waits behind the next prompt's first chunk. Per-request trace shows first tokens land at 0.23, 0.65, 0.87, 0.88s. Stage 1 tested 8,448 against a same-session 8,192 control (5 Oct, stage1/01_chunk_budget_ab, same prompts): 11 of 22 comparable c4 requests land one chunk step (~0.2 s) earlier and 3 one step later; over those 22 the c4 mean falls 13.1% (601.0 → 522.3 ms; the control's two 4.6 s first-wave requests left out) and c32 6.2%. The predicted ~211 ms is one step, not the mean saving.
🧠 Finding 2: MoE Decode Batching Expands Active Experts & Re-binds to Memory
Own step grows 4.5 → 15.8 ms (c1 to c32 at 8K) and 22.9 ms at full load. A batch of 32 is expected to touch ~163 of 256 experts under uniform routing (upper estimate; 222 at full load vs 8 at c1), driving weights read from 0.9 ms to 10.5 and 14.9 ms at memory speed while kernels above the floor stay at 2.5–4.7 ms. By c16, decode is memory-bound again on expert weights.
🔍 Measurement, Model Bounds & Attribution (§7 v1.2)
Totals are measured on every row: client first-token / inter-token time, engine queue, and prefill duration histograms.
Loaded Attribution: Engine decode time matches client (e2e − first token) within 0.4% across all loaded runs. Residual outside queue + prefill is real time outside the engine core. Normal decode step is median token with ITL ≤ 100 ms; remainder is prefill contention delay.
Additive Scope Note: This panel is strictly additive; kernel composition cards, torch profiles, and eager baselines remain untouched. Views 1–4 are the pilot's; the four two-node layouts under load (stage 2, a different session) are in view 5. In the pilot, distributed layouts (TP4/PP2, TP8/PP2, TP4/PP4, TP16/PP1) were run at c1 only, so its loaded points exist on TP4/PP1 and TP8/PP1. Stage 2 ran the distributed layouts under load (8K c8, 128K c2/c4/c8, 1M c2/c4; stage2/03_multi_node_load, 6 Oct) with FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE with autotune off (pilot: Triton) and a different vLLM build, on other GPUs of the same type.
🌊 Technical Clarification on "Waves" (§7)
1. vLLM V1 Engine Waves (DP/EP Coordination): In vLLM V1, a wave coordinates data-parallel workers with expert parallelism via lockstep steps and dummy forward passes. This campaign ran DP = 1, EP = 1 (see Evidence tab), so no dummy-step or lockstep waves existed.
2. GPU Kernel SM Wave Quantization: Tail wave SM under-utilization at small batch (e.g. GEMV running at 43% memory bandwidth) lives inside the "kernels above memory floor" segment, not beside it (requires NCU targeted profiling).

⚖️ PyTorch Operator Attribution: TP4 vs TP8 Decode Breakdown
Self CUDA Time (ms), rank 0, from torch/profiler_out_0.txt — TP4 vs TP8 Decode Trade-off in Interactive Serving (8K Decode)
PYTORCH PROFILER
Grouping Recipe (from trace regexes): Attn (fusedKimiK3MLADecode), MoE (fused_moe_kernel / single_group_topk), AllReduce (ncclDevKernel_AllReduce_Sum_bf16_RING_LL), GEMV (gemvx / cutlass_80_tensorop_gemm), KDA (fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode_kernel / _causal_conv1d_update_kernel), Norm (fused_add_rms_norm).
Rank 0 throughout: the attention, norm and KDA bars are the rank-0 self CUDA time of the kernels in the recipe above (TP4 1.9 / 2.5 / 15.4 ms; TP8 1.8 / 2.7 / 14.8 ms). The earlier 42.1 / 34.8 / 18.2 ms bars and the 519.0 / 739.1 ms sums reproduced from no profiler_out_*.txt and are removed. The AllReduce and GEMV bars are decode-only; the MoE bar covers all 128 steps, the prefill step included.
Operator AccountingTP8 decode-only AllReduce penalty (+277.5 ms; +39.7 µs/call over 6,985 decode calls) exceeds GEMV savings (−44.6 ms: 171.2 → 126.5 ms)
Ring Overhead vs NUMATP8 decode AllReduce takes 58.7 µs vs 18.9 µs (graphs-on torch); 14-step vs 6-step ring adds +17 µs, socket crossing adds ≤ 0.4 µs (nvbandwidth)
MoE & MLPFused MoE kernel time is identical (120ms on TP4 vs 118ms on TP8)
PrescriptionTP4 is already co-located on Socket 0 (GPUs 0–3). Stage 1 pinned each TP8 rank's threads to its GPU's socket (stage1/04_tp8_pinning, against an unpinned control on the same server): TPOT −0.7%, so CPU-thread affinity does not explain the ~21 µs per AllReduce call that TP8 serving adds over nccl-tests (≈1.2 ms per token); the cause stays open.

🧭 Empirical Profiler Observations → Workload-Scoped Architectural Takeaways
Causal mechanisms directly substantiated by Nsight kernel-summary CSV tables & PyTorch call logs
ACTIONABLE DEPLOYMENT RULES
Empirical ObservationCross-Validated Mechanism / ContributorWorkload-Scoped Candidate TakeawaySupporting Artifact
TP4 Decode beats TP8 (-29.5% TPOT @ 8K c1) Canonical matched 8K context baseline: TP4 4.475ms vs TP8 6.350ms (TP4 ~29.5% lower TPOT). Under graphs-on serving, TP8 14-step ring AllReduce barrier latency increases to 58.7 µs vs 18.9 µs on TP4 (3.23 ms vs 1.04 ms collective budget; +17 µs from longer ring, socket crossing adds ≤ 0.4 µs), canceling out GEMV speedup. Single-Node Interactive Serving: For interactive decode serving: Co-locating TP4 workers within a single socket/ring avoids 14-step ring AllReduce latency; pinning each TP8 rank's threads to its GPU's socket (stage 1, stage1/04_tp8_pinning, against an unpinned control on the same server) changed TPOT by only −0.7%, so CPU-thread affinity is ruled out; the cause of the ~21 µs per-call serving gap stays open. profiles_torch_single_node/ (graphs-on torch profiles)
TP8 Prefill beats TP4 (-12% @ 512K, -20% @ 1M) At 512K, TTFT drops from 31.92s to 28.09s (-12.0%) and at 1M from 93.25s to 74.69s (-19.9%). Note: At 128K, TP8 is slightly slower than TP4 in serving (4.81s vs 4.53s). TP8 reduces measured FlashAttention kernel duration in captured profile (6.24ms to 4.26ms). Single-Node Batch / Document Ingestion: For long-context prefill workloads (512K+), evaluate TP8 where prompt processing latency dominates. tp8_prefill/cuda_gpu_kern_sum.csv
TP4/PP4 Dist beats TP16/PP1 (2.4x speedup @ 1M) Pipeline Parallelism transmits sequential activations via P2P SendRecv (8.3% of stage work). TP16 ranks show high aggregate AllReduce kernel-work share (77.6% mean of 12 usable ranks; 76.3–79.5% per rank). 27 hidden layers (20 KDA, 7 full attention). Multi-Node Cloud Deployment: For multi-node cloud deployments on TCP/IP VPC, candidate topology favors Pipeline Parallelism (TP4/PP4 or TP8/PP2) over cross-node Tensor Parallelism (TP16) for tested workloads. tp4_pp4_dist/prefill_128k vs tp16_pp1_dist/prefill_128k
Flat 1M c4 max_num_seqs (~232.3s) TTFT is flat across max_num_seqs 4/8/16 (~232.3s) and peak_running never approaches those configured ceilings; max_num_seqs is non-binding in this tested regime. Tuning Discipline: Do not spend time tuning scheduler sequence limits on extreme-context workloads when running below ceiling. Optimize prompt chunk size and enable prefix reuse. tp4_1m_maxseq4..16/bench.json
Host Launch Gap (3.47s in cudaLaunchKernel) CPU driver launch overhead averages 3.9 μs per kernel; across 888,504 kernel launches, host scheduling overhead accumulates to 31.2% of CPU time. Runtime Optimization: Serving already operates with CUDA Graphs ON (4.47 ms decode step vs 30.5 ms in eager profiler). tp4_decode/cuda_api_sum.csv

server_ready − server_start in every case_manifest.json across 44 case manifests (41 servers reached ready; 3 exited rc=1 before ready). Answers model loading, disk-to-VRAM copy, and CUDA graph capture overhead.

Campaign Summary: Over the whole campaign, 1.25 hours of 4.92 hours of total server-up time was start-up and CUDA-graph compilation (25%). Where a launch's first benchmark ran one request at a time without warm-ups (7 launches: three TP16, three TP4/PP1 and one TP8/PP1; the prefix suite, cold by design, left out), its first request after server-ready came in −0.02% to +3.4% off the median of the later requests (off the second request where a run sent only two) — consistent with CUDA graph capture and compilation completing before server_ready. The other launches ran warm-ups or concurrent load first, so their first request is not measured.

NOT_CAPTURED Reconciliation
E2E Ledger: 7 runs attempted; server stopped with RuntimeError('server exited rc=1') after 126–134s; the pilot archive keeps no server log for any case, so the cause is unlogged. Not resolved in stage 2: the FP8 rerun (stage2/01_fp8_kv_rerun, 6 Oct) exited rc=1 after 184 s, again with no log; offload ran only as a changed case (8.5 GiB GPU KV, prefix caching on; stage2/02_cpu_offload_reuse), and that server started, which fits a KV floor near one 1,048,576-token sequence (7.88 GiB at 8,064 B per token; inferred) but does not log the pilot failure's cause.
Profiler Matrix: 14 captured (8 with usable rank exports, all prefill); 8 missing (3 native batched-decode captures with 0-byte node reports; 5 capped profiles uncaptured in the pilot, no reason recorded; stage 2 captured all five with every rank usable: stage2/05_capped_profiles, 6 Oct). Stage 2's TP16 512K re-capture (stage2/06_tp16_512k_prefill, 16 of 16 ranks usable) also made that point usable: 19 of 22 points are captured and 14 have usable exports.

Provenance / Statistical Guardrails
Baseline vs Performance Characterization: never silently merge. Every row carries suite_version, run_id, model revision, runtime version, network provenance and evidence class. Compare only sufficiently matched workloads.
Percentiles: promote p95 only when completed sample count ≥ 20; promote p99 only when completed sample count ≥ 100. Raw low-N percentile fields may exist but must not be presented as reliable SLO statistics.
Evidence classes: DIRECT_MEASURED · TIMELINE_ATTRIBUTED · DERIVED · UNRESOLVED.
